lesson.title: The Great Law of Peace: How Five Nations Became One
lesson.summary: This section explains the formation and government of the Haudenosaunee, or Iroquois Confederacy, a political union of Native nations in the Northeast whose Great Law of Peace bound five, later six, independent nations under a shared council.
lesson.body:
In the woodlands of what is now New York State, five nations, the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca, came together to form one of the most enduring political institutions in North American history: the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, often called the Iroquois Confederacy by outsiders, though the people themselves use Haudenosaunee, meaning people of the longhouse, a term that reflects both their traditional architecture and the way they understood their union, as a single symbolic longhouse sheltering five related nations. These were farming and hunting societies, building on the same agricultural traditions of corn, beans, and squash found throughout the Northeast Woodlands culture area.

According to Haudenosaunee oral tradition, the confederacy was founded by a spiritual figure known as the Peacemaker, working alongside a leader named Hiawatha, who traveled among warring nations to convince them to give up cycles of blood feud and revenge in favor of a shared system of law and diplomacy. Historians and archaeologists continue to debate exactly when this founding took place, with estimates ranging from as early as the twelfth century to as late as the sixteenth, since the tradition was preserved orally and through wampum belts rather than written records. What is well documented is the durability of the resulting institution, which endured for centuries and eventually expanded when the Tuscarora nation, migrating north after conflict with English colonists, joined around 1722, transforming the Five Nations into the Six Nations.

At the heart of the confederacy was a body of law known as the Great Law of Peace, which established a Grand Council of representatives, called sachems, from each member nation, who met to resolve disputes and coordinate action while leaving each nation self governing in most internal matters. Notably, the confederacy operated on a matrilineal clan system, in which women held significant political authority. Clan mothers selected and could remove sachems from office, a striking contrast to the political systems of contemporary European states, where women were almost entirely excluded from formal governance.

The Haudenosaunee Confederacy was not merely symbolic. It functioned as a real military and diplomatic power, capable of coordinating the actions of its member nations against outside threats and negotiating collectively with European colonial governments once contact began. Colonial officials, including Benjamin Franklin, who observed Haudenosaunee diplomacy at negotiations in Lancaster, Pennsylvania in 1744 and referenced the confederacy's structure in his own later writings on colonial union, took note of how effectively it balanced local autonomy with collective strength, though historians continue to debate how much direct influence Haudenosaunee political ideas had on later American constitutional thought.

The Haudenosaunee Confederacy shows that sophisticated, durable political institutions developed independently in North America, built on principles, federalism, checks on individual power, and a formal peace process, that would later be recognizable to students of any government. It stands alongside the Mississippian mound building societies discussed earlier as further evidence of the political and social complexity that existed across the continent long before, and well after, European colonization began.
